claim: Combined genetic deficiency of three clusters in the miR-17~92 family drastically shifted macrophage phenotypes toward the inflammatory spectrum characterized by heightened production of pro-inflammatory mediator TNF and diminished expression of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
source: Combined genetic deficiency of three clusters in the miR-17~92 family drastically shifted macrophage phenotypes toward the inflammatory spectrum characterized by heightened production of pro-inflammatory mediator TNF and diminished expression of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing altered cytokine expression in TKO macrophages as presented in the manuscript.

claim: Macrophages residing in the adipose tissues from myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice spontaneously developed inflammatory phenotypes.
source: Consequently, macrophages residing in the adipose tissues from myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice spontaneously developed inflammatory phenotypes and displayed alterations of overall physiological conditions as evidenced by obesity and compromised glucose tolerance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATM analysis in TKO mice showing inflammatory gene expression patterns.

claim: Myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice displayed obesity.
source: Consequently, macrophages residing in the adipose tissues from myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice spontaneously developed inflammatory phenotypes and displayed alterations of overall physiological conditions as evidenced by obesity and compromised glucose tolerance.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements, VAT weight measurements, and MRI data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice displayed compromised glucose tolerance.
source: Consequently, macrophages residing in the adipose tissues from myeloid-specific miRNA triple knockout mice spontaneously developed inflammatory phenotypes and displayed alterations of overall physiological conditions as evidenced by obesity and compromised glucose tolerance.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs sustained IL-10 production by promoting transcription of the Fos gene.
source: Mechanistically, miR-17~92 family miRNAs sustained IL-10 production by promoting transcription of the Fos gene, which is secondary to downregulation of Fos by transcription factor YY1, a direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Fos expression levels in WT vs TKO cells and rescue experiments with Fos overexpression.

claim: YY1 is a direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
source: Mechanistically, miR-17~92 family miRNAs sustained IL-10 production by promoting transcription of the Fos gene, which is secondary to downregulation of Fos by transcription factor YY1, a direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assays showing direct binding of miR-17 family miRNAs to YY1 3'UTR and increased YY1 protein in TKO cells.

claim: YY1 downregulates Fos transcription.
source: Mechanistically, miR-17~92 family miRNAs sustained IL-10 production by promoting transcription of the Fos gene, which is secondary to downregulation of Fos by transcription factor YY1, a direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments showing increased Fos expression when YY1 is reduced, and by citation to previous literature (Shi et al., 1997).

claim: TKO mice consistently exhibited increased body weights than age- and gender-matched Lyz2-Cre (WT) control mice at the age of 30 weeks.
source: Interestingly, we found that TKO mice consistently exhibited increased body weights than age- and gender-matched Lyz2-Cre (WT) control mice at the age of 30 weeks (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: The absolute weights of VAT and BAT in TKO mice were significantly higher than those in WT mice.
source: Then we isolated the visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT) from these mice and found that both the absolute weights of VAT and BAT and the percentages of VAT in TKO mice were significantly higher than those in WT mice (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue weight measurements shown in Figure 1B, C and supplementary figures.

claim: The percentages of VAT in TKO mice were significantly higher than those in WT mice.
source: Then we isolated the visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT) from these mice and found that both the absolute weights of VAT and BAT and the percentages of VAT in TKO mice were significantly higher than those in WT mice (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by percentage calculations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The total adipose tissue weight and its percentage of body weight were significantly increased in TKO mice as measured by MRI.
source: Furthermore, we scanned these mice with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and found that the total adipose tissue weight and its percentage of body weight were significantly increased in TKO mice (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI measurements shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs protected mice from obesity.
source: Thus, these results indicated that miR-17~92 family miRNAs protected mice from obesity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the obesity phenotype observed in TKO mice lacking these miRNAs.

claim: Body weights, VAT weights, and the VAT percentages of TKO mice were significantly higher than those of WT mice upon 20 weeks of feeding with high fat-diet.
source: Consistent with the results obtained with animals under regular diet, body weights, VAT weights, and the VAT percentages of TKO mice were significantly higher than those of WT mice upon 20 weeks of feeding with high fat-diet (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from HFD-fed mice shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Both total adipose tissue weight and its percentage were significantly increased in TKO mice fed with high-fat diet as measured by MRI.
source: Meanwhile, TKO and WT mice were scanned with MRI, and MRI quantitation indicated that both total adipose tissue weight and its percentage were significantly increased in TKO mice (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI data from HFD-fed mice shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: TKO chimeric mice exhibited increased body weights compared with WT chimeric mice.
source: TKO chimeric mice also exhibited increased body weights compared with WT chimeric mice (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements from bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The absolute weights and the percentages of VAT and total adipose tissue were significantly increased in TKO chimeric mice.
source: Moreover, the absolute weights and the percentages of VAT and total adipose tissue were significantly increased in TKO chimeric mice (Figure 1L–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue weight and percentage measurements from chimeric mice shown in Figure 1L-O.

claim: Myeloid-intrinsic miR-17~92 family miRNAs protect mice from obesity.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that myeloid-intrinsic miR-17~92 family miRNAs protect mice from obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by bone marrow chimera experiments demonstrating the cell-intrinsic role of these miRNAs.

claim: TKO mice showed higher insulin resistance than control animals.
source: As obesity is often associated with insulin resistance, we first examined the glucose homeostasis in TKO and WT mice with glucose tolerance test (GTT) and found that TKO mice showed higher insulin resistance than control animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF and anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 are critical in regulating the insulin sensitivity and obesity.
source: It is well established that pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF and anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 are critical in regulating the insulin sensitivity and obesity (Chawla et al., 2011; Olefsky and Glass, 2010), so we first detected TNF and IL-10 levels in the serum of WT and TKO mice and found increased TNF and decreased IL-10 proteins in TKO mice relative to WT animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chawla et al., 2011; Olefsky and Glass, 2010).

claim: TKO mice had increased TNF and decreased IL-10 proteins in serum relative to WT animals.
source: It is well established that pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF and anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 are critical in regulating the insulin sensitivity and obesity (Chawla et al., 2011; Olefsky and Glass, 2010), so we first detected TNF and IL-10 levels in the serum of WT and TKO mice and found increased TNF and decreased IL-10 proteins in TKO mice relative to WT animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The expression of Tnf was significantly higher in TKO VAT than in WT VAT.
source: We found that the expression of Tnf was significantly higher, whereas the expression of Il10 was significantly lower in TKO VAT than those in WT VAT (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from VAT tissue shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: The expression of Il10 was significantly lower in TKO VAT than in WT VAT.
source: We found that the expression of Tnf was significantly higher, whereas the expression of Il10 was significantly lower in TKO VAT than those in WT VAT (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from VAT tissue shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: Macrophages are the major immune cells producing TNF and IL-10 cytokines in the VAT.
source: As macrophages are reported to be the major immune cells producing these cytokines in the VAT (Chawla et al., 2011; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011), we first analyzed the ATM population in VAT of WT and TKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chawla et al., 2011; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011).

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs were efficiently deleted in TKO ATMs.
source: miR-17~92 family miRNAs were efficiently deleted in TKO ATMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–E) and their deficiency did not alter the population of ATMs in mice (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing miRNA expression in ATMs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNA deficiency did not alter the population of ATMs in mice.
source: miR-17~92 family miRNAs were efficiently deleted in TKO ATMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–E) and their deficiency did not alter the population of ATMs in mice (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing ATM populations in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Genes differentially expressed in both TKO versus WT mice and high-fat diet versus chow diet fed WT mice were enriched in the inflammatory response category.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis indicated that genes differentially expressed in both TKO versus WT mice and high-fat diet versus chow diet fed WT mice were enriched in the inflammatory response category (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: ATMs from TKO mice were more inflammatory than the WT counterparts under both regular chow diet and high-fat diet conditions.
source: Meanwhile, the inflammatory score indexing cellular inflammatory phenotypes calculated based on the RNA sequencing data indicated that ATMs from TKO mice were more inflammatory than the WT counterparts under both regular chow diet and high-fat diet conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by inflammatory score calculations from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: TKO ATMs expressed increased Tnf and decreased Il10.
source: Moreover, both RNA sequencing results and qPCR results showed that TKO ATMs expressed increased Tnf and decreased Il10 (Figure 2F–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 2F–H and supplementary figures.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs maintain ATM homeostasis to prevent obesity and to facilitate glucose tolerance.
source: Thus, these results demonstrated that miR-17~92 family miRNA deficiency shifts ATM toward an inflammatory phenotype characterized by TNF overproduction in the absence of exogenous infectious or inflammatory signals, suggesting that miR-17~92 family miRNAs maintain ATM homeostasis to prevent obesity and to facilitate glucose tolerance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of inflammatory ATM phenotype and metabolic consequences in TKO mice.

claim: Basal expression of Tnf mRNA was consistently upregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls.
source: Compared to WT controls, basal expression of Tnf mRNA and of Il10 mRNA was consistently upregulated and downregulated, respectively in TKO BMDMs (Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), recapitulating the above observations in ATMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from BMDMs shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Basal expression of Il10 mRNA was consistently downregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls.
source: Compared to WT controls, basal expression of Tnf mRNA and of Il10 mRNA was consistently upregulated and downregulated, respectively in TKO BMDMs (Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), recapitulating the above observations in ATMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from BMDMs shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: Upregulation or downregulation of Tnf and Il10 expression became more appreciable in activated macrophages than in resting cells.
source: Notably, due to heightened expression of these cytokine genes in TLR-activated especially lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated conditions, upregulation or downregulation of Tnf and Il10 expression became more appreciable in activated macrophages than in resting cells (Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from LPS-stimulated BMDMs shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The mRNA expression patterns were corroborated with alterations of TNF and IL-10 protein production by TKO macrophages.
source: The mRNA expression patterns were further corroborated with alterations of TNF and IL-10 protein production by TKO macrophages (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data showing protein levels in Figure 3E and F.

claim: With sufficient quantity of IL-10, TNF production by TKO BMDMs reduced to a comparable level as WT BMDMs.
source: Next, in order to clarify the connection between TNF and IL-10 in TKO BMDMs, we supplemented recombinant IL-10 protein prior to LPS stimulation and found that with sufficient quantity of IL-10, TNF production by TKO BMDMs reduced to a comparable level as WT BMDMs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data from IL-10 supplementation experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Blockade of IL-10 receptor with an anti-IL-10R antibody prior to LPS stimulation diminished the differences of TNF production observed between WT and TKO BMDMs.
source: Moreover, blockade of IL-10 receptor with an anti-IL-10R antibody prior to LPS stimulation diminished the differences of TNF production observed between WT and TKO BMDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), implying that overexpression of TNF was likely secondary to inadequate amount of IL-10 produced by TKO cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data from IL-10R blockade experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Overexpression of TNF was likely secondary to inadequate amount of IL-10 produced by TKO cells.
source: Moreover, blockade of IL-10 receptor with an anti-IL-10R antibody prior to LPS stimulation diminished the differences of TNF production observed between WT and TKO BMDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), implying that overexpression of TNF was likely secondary to inadequate amount of IL-10 produced by TKO cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IL-10 supplementation and IL-10R blockade experiments.

claim: The anti-TNF treatment significantly reversed the obese phenotypes of TKO mice.
source: To functionally correct the obese phenotypes of TKO mice, an anti-TNF antibody or PBS was administrated weekly to TKO and WT mice along with HFD for 20 weeks. The anti-TNF treatment significantly reversed the obese phenotypes of TKO mice (Figure 3H), indicating that TNF was a functional target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in regulating obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements from anti-TNF treatment experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: TNF was a functional target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in regulating obesity.
source: To functionally correct the obese phenotypes of TKO mice, an anti-TNF antibody or PBS was administrated weekly to TKO and WT mice along with HFD for 20 weeks. The anti-TNF treatment significantly reversed the obese phenotypes of TKO mice (Figure 3H), indicating that TNF was a functional target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in regulating obesity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anti-TNF treatment rescue experiment.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs suppressed TNF-mediated inflammation through promoting IL-10 expression in macrophages.
source: Overall, these results suggested that miR-17~92 family miRNAs suppressed TNF-mediated inflammation through promoting IL-10 expression in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of IL-10 regulation and TNF suppression experiments.

claim: Deletion of individual cluster or double deficiency of miR-106a~363 and miR-106b~25 clusters (DKO) did not significantly alter LPS-induced Tnf expression in macrophages.
source: Deletion of individual cluster or double deficiency of miR-106a~363 and miR-106b~25 clusters (DKO) did not significantly alter LPS-induced Tnf expression in macrophages (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from single and double knockout BMDMs shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Expression of Il10 showed modest reduction in individual cluster single KO as well as in DKO BMDMs.
source: Expression of Il10 showed modest reduction in individual cluster single KO as well as in DKO BMDMs (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from single and double knockout BMDMs shown in Figure 4E–H.

claim: Tnf was only markedly upregulated upon deletion of all three clusters.
source: To investigate the collective effects of these three clusters, we compared the fold changes of Tnf and Il10 expression over their respective WT controls among macrophages harboring various genotypes of miRNA deficiency and found that Tnf was only markedly upregulated upon deletion of all three clusters while the extent of Il10 downregulation largely correlated with the number of deleted miRNA clusters (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative qPCR data from various knockout genotypes shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The extent of Il10 downregulation largely correlated with the number of deleted miRNA clusters.
source: To investigate the collective effects of these three clusters, we compared the fold changes of Tnf and Il10 expression over their respective WT controls among macrophages harboring various genotypes of miRNA deficiency and found that Tnf was only markedly upregulated upon deletion of all three clusters while the extent of Il10 downregulation largely correlated with the number of deleted miRNA clusters (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative qPCR data from various knockout genotypes shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Three miRNA clusters of miR-17~92 family collectively inhibited TNF and promoted IL-10 expression in macrophages.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that three miRNA clusters of miR-17~92 family collectively inhibited TNF and promoted IL-10 expression in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative analysis of single, double, and triple knockout phenotypes.

claim: PTEN is a well-studied target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
source: As phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) is a well-studied target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs (O'Donnell et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 2008) and PTEN and its related molecules have been implicated in modulating IL-10 expression (Hu et al., 2006; Martin et al., 2005), we first investigated whether miR-17~92 family miRNAs regulated IL-10 and TNF through targeting PTEN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (O'Donnell et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 2008).

claim: PTEN and its related molecules have been implicated in modulating IL-10 expression.
source: As phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) is a well-studied target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs (O'Donnell et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 2008) and PTEN and its related molecules have been implicated in modulating IL-10 expression (Hu et al., 2006; Martin et al., 2005), we first investigated whether miR-17~92 family miRNAs regulated IL-10 and TNF through targeting PTEN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Hu et al., 2006; Martin et al., 2005).

claim: Inhibition of PTEN phosphatase activity by a chemical inhibitor in TKO BMDMs did not apparently alter expression of IL-10 and TNF.
source: Inhibition of PTEN phosphatase activity by a chemical inhibitor in TKO BMDMs did not apparently alter expression of IL-10 and TNF, suggesting that the regulation of TNF and IL-10 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs was independent of PTEN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from PTEN inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The regulation of TNF and IL-10 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs was independent of PTEN.
source: Inhibition of PTEN phosphatase activity by a chemical inhibitor in TKO BMDMs did not apparently alter expression of IL-10 and TNF, suggesting that the regulation of TNF and IL-10 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs was independent of PTEN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PTEN inhibitor experiments showing no effect on cytokine expression.

claim: Fos encodes a key component of transcriptional factor AP-1 that drives the expression of IL-10.
source: Interestingly, we found that Fos, encoding a key component of transcriptional factor AP-1 that drives the expression of IL-10 (Hu et al., 2006; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010), was downregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls, whereas the expression of other reported targets of miR-17~92 family miRNAs remained minimally affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Hu et al., 2006; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010).

claim: Fos was downregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls.
source: Interestingly, we found that Fos, encoding a key component of transcriptional factor AP-1 that drives the expression of IL-10 (Hu et al., 2006; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010), was downregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls, whereas the expression of other reported targets of miR-17~92 family miRNAs remained minimally affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The expression of other reported targets of miR-17~92 family miRNAs remained minimally affected in TKO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, we found that Fos, encoding a key component of transcriptional factor AP-1 that drives the expression of IL-10 (Hu et al., 2006; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010), was downregulated in TKO BMDMs compared to WT controls, whereas the expression of other reported targets of miR-17~92 family miRNAs remained minimally affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing minimal changes in other known targets shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fos was consistently and significantly decreased in TKO BMDMs at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: Then we experimentally confirmed that Fos was consistently and significantly decreased in TKO BMDMs at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B–E and supplementary figures.

claim: The expression of Jun did not apparently differ between WT and TKO BMDMs.
source: In contrast to Fos, the expression of Jun, another key component of AP-1 complex, did not apparently differ between WT and TKO BMDMs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Overexpression of Fos in TKO BMDMs rescued the reduced expression of IL-10 and the enhanced expression of TNF to the levels comparable with that in WT cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Fos in TKO BMDMs rescued the reduced expression of IL-10 and the enhanced expression of TNF to the levels comparable with that in WT cells (Figure 5F–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B), indicating that subdued expression of IL-10 in TKO BMDMs was likely resulted from diminished Fos activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and ELISA data from Fos overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5F–H and supplementary figures.

claim: Subdued expression of IL-10 in TKO BMDMs was likely resulted from diminished Fos activities.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Fos in TKO BMDMs rescued the reduced expression of IL-10 and the enhanced expression of TNF to the levels comparable with that in WT cells (Figure 5F–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B), indicating that subdued expression of IL-10 in TKO BMDMs was likely resulted from diminished Fos activities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Fos overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs promoted IL-10 production via sustaining the expression of Fos.
source: Thus, these data demonstrated that miR-17~92 family miRNAs promoted IL-10 production via sustaining the expression of Fos.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of Fos downregulation in TKO cells and rescue by Fos overexpression.

claim: Fos is reported to be inhibited by a transcriptional factor YY1.
source: In previous studies, Fos is reported to be inhibited by a transcriptional factor YY1 (Shi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Shi et al., 1997).

claim: The mRNA levels of Yy1 were comparable between WT and TKO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, despite the fact that the mRNA levels of Yy1 were comparable between WT and TKO BMDMs, YY1 protein was significantly increased in TKO BMDMs (Figure 6A–C), implying post-transcriptional regulation of YY1 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YY1 protein was significantly increased in TKO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, despite the fact that the mRNA levels of Yy1 were comparable between WT and TKO BMDMs, YY1 protein was significantly increased in TKO BMDMs (Figure 6A–C), implying post-transcriptional regulation of YY1 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: YY1 is subject to post-transcriptional regulation by miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
source: Interestingly, despite the fact that the mRNA levels of Yy1 were comparable between WT and TKO BMDMs, YY1 protein was significantly increased in TKO BMDMs (Figure 6A–C), implying post-transcriptional regulation of YY1 by miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels of YY1 in TKO cells.

claim: YY1 is a predicted target of the miR-17 family miRNAs.
source: Bioinformatics analysis with the miRanda tool (Betel et al., 2010) revealed YY1 as a predicted target of the miR-17 family miRNAs, a subfamily of miR-17~92 family miRNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics prediction using miRanda tool and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Luciferase reporter assays with the constructs containing Yy1 3′UTR showed significant attenuation of luciferase activities by miRNAs from miR-17~92, miR-106a~363, or miR-106b~25 cluster.
source: Luciferase reporter assays with the constructs containing Yy1 3′UTR showed significant attenuation of luciferase activities by miRNAs from miR-17~92, miR-106a~363, or miR-106b~25 cluster, whereas mutation of the miR-17 family miRNAs' binding sites on Yy1 3'UTR reversed such inhibitory effects (Figure 6E), suggesting that YY1 was likely to be the direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Mutation of the miR-17 family miRNAs' binding sites on Yy1 3'UTR reversed the inhibitory effects on luciferase activity.
source: Luciferase reporter assays with the constructs containing Yy1 3′UTR showed significant attenuation of luciferase activities by miRNAs from miR-17~92, miR-106a~363, or miR-106b~25 cluster, whereas mutation of the miR-17 family miRNAs' binding sites on Yy1 3'UTR reversed such inhibitory effects (Figure 6E), suggesting that YY1 was likely to be the direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated constructs shown in Figure 6E.

claim: YY1 is likely to be the direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
source: Luciferase reporter assays with the constructs containing Yy1 3′UTR showed significant attenuation of luciferase activities by miRNAs from miR-17~92, miR-106a~363, or miR-106b~25 cluster, whereas mutation of the miR-17 family miRNAs' binding sites on Yy1 3'UTR reversed such inhibitory effects (Figure 6E), suggesting that YY1 was likely to be the direct target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results showing direct binding.

claim: Knocking down YY1 significantly upregulated the expression of Fos at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Knocking down YY1 significantly upregulated the expression of Fos at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 6F–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) and subsequently decreased TNF and increased IL-10 expression (Figure 6I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and immunoblotting data from YY1 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6F–H and supplementary figures.

claim: Knocking down YY1 subsequently decreased TNF and increased IL-10 expression.
source: Knocking down YY1 significantly upregulated the expression of Fos at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 6F–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B) and subsequently decreased TNF and increased IL-10 expression (Figure 6I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and ELISA data from YY1 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6I–L.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs promoted Fos expression by releasing YY1-mediated inhibition.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that miR-17~92 family miRNAs promoted Fos expression by releasing YY1-mediated inhibition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of YY1 as a target of miR-17~92 family miRNAs and YY1's inhibition of Fos.

claim: Global deficiency of the miR-17~92 cluster results in embryonic lethality.
source: Genetic studies have shown that global deficiency of the miR-17~92 cluster results in embryonic lethality, whereas deletion of miR-106a~363 or miR-25~363 cluster yields no apparent phenotypes (Ventura et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ventura et al., 2008).

claim: Deletion of miR-106a~363 or miR-25~363 cluster yields no apparent phenotypes.
source: Genetic studies have shown that global deficiency of the miR-17~92 cluster results in embryonic lethality, whereas deletion of miR-106a~363 or miR-25~363 cluster yields no apparent phenotypes (Ventura et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ventura et al., 2008).

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs play an important role in developmental processes and are regarded as oncogenes during tumorigenesis.
source: Functionally, miR-17~92 family miRNAs play an important role in developmental processes and are regarded as oncogenes during tumorigenesis (Mendell, 2008; Mogilyansky and Rigoutsos, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mendell, 2008; Mogilyansky and Rigoutsos, 2013).

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs have been implicated in the maintenance of lymphocyte homeostasis, regulation of T follicular helper cell differentiation, and modulation of B cell development.
source: In the immune system, miR-17~92 family miRNAs have been implicated in the maintenance of lymphocyte homeostasis, regulation of T follicular helper cell differentiation, and modulation of B cell development (Kang et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kang et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2008).

claim: Relatively little is known about the functions of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in myeloid cells including macrophages.
source: However, relatively little is known about the functions of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in myeloid cells including macrophages.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on literature review.

claim: The spectrum of macrophage phenotypes could be partially attributed to the relative quantities of pro- versus anti-inflammatory mediators such as the antagonizing TNF-IL-10 pair.
source: The spectrum of phenotypes could be partially attributed to the relative quantities of pro- versus anti-inflammatory mediators such as the antagonizing TNF-IL-10 pair (Mosser and Edwards, 2008; Sugimoto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mosser and Edwards, 2008; Sugimoto et al., 2019).

claim: Disruption of the balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines has been causally linked with pathogenesis of an array of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
source: The production of these pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines is tightly controlled to achieve an intricate balance, and disruption of such balance has been causally linked with pathogenesis of an array of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD; Bain and Mowat, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Bain and Mowat, 2014).

claim: During the development of obesity, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF promote insulin resistance in adipose tissue.
source: For example, during the development of obesity, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF promote insulin resistance in adipose tissue (Chawla et al., 2011; Olefsky and Glass, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chawla et al., 2011; Olefsky and Glass, 2010).

claim: In the obese adipose tissues, macrophages are the most abundant infiltrating immune cells and the major source of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: In the obese adipose tissues, macrophages are the most abundant infiltrating immune cells and the major source of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Chawla et al., 2011; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chawla et al., 2011; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011).

claim: The proper macrophage phenotypes in the adipose tissue microenvironment are critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis.
source: Thus, the proper macrophage phenotypes in the adipose tissue microenvironment are critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the established role of macrophages in adipose tissue and metabolic regulation.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs consist of three paralogous miRNA clusters that encode in total 13 distinct mature miRNAs.
source: miR-17~92 family miRNAs consist of three paralogous miRNA clusters (Mirc1 [called 'miR-17~92' here], Mirc2 [called 'miR-106a~363' here], and Mirc3 [called 'miR-106b~25' here]) that encode in total 13 distinct mature miRNAs, which can be further divided into four subfamilies (miR-17, miR-18, miR-19, and miR-25) according to their seed regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Mendell, 2008; Ventura et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by schematic representation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B and citations to previous literature.

claim: The 13 distinct mature miRNAs of miR-17~92 family can be further divided into four subfamilies (miR-17, miR-18, miR-19, and miR-25) according to their seed regions.
source: miR-17~92 family miRNAs consist of three paralogous miRNA clusters (Mirc1 [called 'miR-17~92' here], Mirc2 [called 'miR-106a~363' here], and Mirc3 [called 'miR-106b~25' here]) that encode in total 13 distinct mature miRNAs, which can be further divided into four subfamilies (miR-17, miR-18, miR-19, and miR-25) according to their seed regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Mendell, 2008; Ventura et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence information in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations to previous literature.

claim: MicroRNAs are a class of short non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally in metazoan organisms.
source: MicroRNAs are a class of short non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally in metazoan organisms.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about microRNA function.

claim: miRNAs are processed from their primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs) that are cleaved by enzymes Drosha and DiGeorge syndrome critical region gene 8 (DGCR8) into ~70 nucleotide precursors (pre-miRNAs) that are further processed by Dicer into the ~22 nucleotide long mature miRNAs.
source: miRNAs are processed from their primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs) that are cleaved by enzymes Drosha and DiGeorge syndrome critical region gene 8 (DGCR8) into ~70 nucleotide precursors (pre-miRNAs) that are further processed by Dicer into the ~22 nucleotide long mature miRNAs (Krol et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Krol et al., 2010).

claim: For approximately 25–40% of miRNAs, their precursors are located in close proximity to other neighboring precursors on chromatin to form miRNA clusters.
source: For approximately 25–40% of miRNAs, their precursors are located in close proximity to other neighboring precursors on chromatin to form miRNA clusters (Altuvia et al., 2005; Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014), which typically yield mature miRNAs with distinct seed regions that may act coordinately to achieve common functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Altuvia et al., 2005; Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014).

claim: miRNA clusters typically yield mature miRNAs with distinct seed regions that may act coordinately to achieve common functions.
source: For approximately 25–40% of miRNAs, their precursors are located in close proximity to other neighboring precursors on chromatin to form miRNA clusters (Altuvia et al., 2005; Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014), which typically yield mature miRNAs with distinct seed regions that may act coordinately to achieve common functions.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about miRNA cluster function.

claim: TNF-activated signaling molecules such as IKK, JNK, S6 kinase, and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) could potentially phosphorylate insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) to attenuate insulin signaling and subsequently contribute to the development of insulin resistance.
source: For example, TNF-activated signaling molecules such as IKK, JNK, S6 kinase, and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) could potentially phosphorylate insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) to attenuate insulin signaling and subsequently contribute to the development of insulin resistance (Gao et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2003; Hirosumi et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2007; Ozes et al., 2001; Yin et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature (Gao et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2003; Hirosumi et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2007; Ozes et al., 2001; Yin et al., 1998).

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs have been reported to regulate adipocyte development.
source: Although miR-17~92 family miRNAs have been reported to regulate adipocyte development (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2008), the current study depicted a miR-17~92 family miRNA-centric immune circuit operative in macrophages that indirectly controls metabolic phenotypes such as insulin resistance and obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2008).

claim: Previous studies have validated multiple targets of miR-17~92 family miRNAs including E2F1, PTEN, Bim, PHLPP2, and C/EBPβ.
source: Previous studies have implicated the roles of miR-17~92 family miRNAs in developmental processes and tumorigenesis (Mendell, 2008; Mogilyansky and Rigoutsos, 2013), and validated multiple targets including E2F1 (O'Donnell et al., 2005), PTEN (O'Donnell et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 2008), Bim (Ventura et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2008), PHLPP2 (Kang et al., 2013), and C/EBPβ (Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature (O'Donnell et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 2008; Ventura et al., 2008; Kang et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2020).

claim: IL-10 is a potent anti-inflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in resolution of inflammation and robustly suppresses production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF via transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: IL-10 is a potent anti-inflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in resolution of inflammation and robustly suppresses production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF via transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms (Moore et al., 2001; Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Moore et al., 2001; Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019).

claim: Full-fledged expression of IL-10 by macrophages is achieved by coordinated action of transcription factors including c-Maf and AP-1.
source: Full-fledged expression of IL-10 by macrophages is achieved by coordinated action of transcription factors including c-Maf and AP-1 (Cao et al., 2005; Ouyang et al., 2011; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cao et al., 2005; Ouyang et al., 2011; Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010).

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs are key positive regulators supporting IL-10 production in ATMs.
source: Here we identified miR-17~92 family miRNAs as key positive regulators supporting IL-10 production in ATMs, raising possibilities for this family of miRNAs as potential therapeutic targets of inflammatory and metabolic disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing IL-10 regulation by these miRNAs.

claim: miR-17~92 family miRNAs are potential therapeutic targets of inflammatory and metabolic disorders.
source: Here we identified miR-17~92 family miRNAs as key positive regulators supporting IL-10 production in ATMs, raising possibilities for this family of miRNAs as potential therapeutic targets of inflammatory and metabolic disorders.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the functional role of these miRNAs in regulating inflammation and metabolism.
